title: "Assignment 5: Visualization Audit"
author: "Jade Lee"
---

## Question

How did mean BMI differ between women and men aged 20-80 across NHANES cycles in the prepared class dataset?

## Load the data

```{r}
#| message: false
library(tidyverse)

nhanes <- read_csv("examples/nhanes-equity/data/nhanes_equity_v6.csv",
                   show_col_types = FALSE)
```

## Check exclusions

```{r}
nhanes |>
  filter(Age >= 20, Age <= 80) |>
  summarise(
    adults_20_80 = n(),
    missing_bmi = sum(is.na(BMI)),
    missing_gender = sum(is.na(Gender))
  )
```

Of 57,137 adults aged 20-80, 1,009 (about 1.8%) had missing BMI and were excluded. No records were missing gender.

## Descriptive summary

```{r}
# AI prompt: change the income summary to gender, adults 20-80, all cycles
# Verified: 22 rows (11 cycles x 2 genders); the smallest group has 1,923 people

bmi_by_gender <- nhanes |>
  filter(!is.na(BMI), Age >= 20, Age <= 80) |>
  group_by(Cycle, Gender) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean_bmi = round(mean(BMI), 2), .groups = "drop")

bmi_by_gender
```

## Draft plot

```{r}
# AI prompt: line plot of mean BMI by cycle, one line per gender, y-axis from 0
# Verified: 22 points match bmi_by_gender; lines look almost flat
draft_plot <- ggplot(bmi_by_gender,
                     aes(x = Cycle, y = mean_bmi, color = Gender, group = Gender)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  expand_limits(y = 0)

draft_plot
```

My first draft had three problems:

- The y-axis started at 0, so the lines looked almost flat and the changes of about 1-2 BMI units across cycles were hard to see.
- The cycle labels on the x-axis overlapped and could not be read.
- It had no title, subtitle, or caption, and the y-axis label was the raw variable name (`mean_bmi`). A reader could not tell that the plot showed adults only or that the summary was unweighted.

## Corrected plot

```{r}
#| fig-cap: "Mean BMI by gender across NHANES cycles, adults aged 20-80 in the prepared NHANES Health Equity class dataset. The summary is descriptive and unweighted. Records with missing BMI were excluded. There is no 2019-2020 cycle. The y-axis starts at 27, not 0, to show changes of about 1-2 BMI units; BMI cannot be 0, and a line chart compares positions, not bar lengths. The plot shows patterns, not causal effects or population estimates."

# AI prompt: x-axis labels overlap and the lines look flat with the y-axis at 0. fix both without removing data
# Verified: x-axis labels are readable after rotating; I compared the plot with y from 0 and from 27 and kept 27 because the ups and downs were visible; points match bmi_by_gender


final_plot <- ggplot(bmi_by_gender,
                     aes(x = Cycle, y = mean_bmi, color = Gender, group = Gender)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(27, 31)) +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Dark2") +
  labs(
    title = "Mean BMI by gender across NHANES cycles",
    subtitle = "Adults age 20-80 in the prepared class dataset; unweighted descriptive summary",
    x = "NHANES cycle",
    y = "Mean BMI (kg/m²)",
    color = "Gender",
    caption = "Unweighted. Excludes missing BMI. No 2019-2020 cycle.\nY-axis starts at 27 to show changes of about 1-2 BMI units."
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
    legend.position = "bottom"
  )

final_plot

ggsave(
  "assignments/assignment05-visualization/submission/corrected-plot.png",
  plot = final_plot,
  width = 7,
  height = 5
)
```


## What changed and why

I compared women and men because Gender has no missing values and both groups are large in every cycle, so the comparison adds no extra exclusions and has no small groups.

I applied the lessons from auditing the flawed plot to my own draft. I kept only adults aged 20-80, because the flawed plot said "adults" but included children as young as 2. I used all 11 cycles instead of two endpoints, so the reader sees the real ups and downs.

In my draft, the y-axis started at 0 and the lines looked almost flat, so the changes across cycles were hard to see. Because BMI cannot be 0 and a line chart compares positions rather than bar lengths, I zoomed in to 27-31 instead. I used `coord_cartesian()`, which zooms without removing data, and I stated the axis choice in the caption. The flawed plot also zoomed in, but it hid that choice and paired it with causal wording.

The title describes what is plotted without claiming a cause. The subtitle and caption state that the summary is unweighted and that 1,009 adults with missing BMI were excluded.
